questions.enonce_markdown:
The Groups I and II elements are known as the s-block elements.

(i) State and explain how atomic radius varies down the Group I elements.

(ii) List the Group II elements in order of increasing atomic number.

(iii) Why is potassium carbonate readily soluble in water whereas calcium carbonate is insoluble?

(iv) Write chemical equations to show the product(s) formed when potassium and barium are heated in excess oxygen.

A: Potassium (K)

B: Barium (Ba) *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The atomic radius **increases** down Group I (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs). Each element has **one more occupied electron shell** than the one above, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus. The increase in nuclear charge is more than offset by the increased shielding of the outer electron by the extra inner shells, so the attraction on the outer electron is weaker and the atom is larger.

**(ii)** Beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, radium: **Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra**.

**(iii)** Whether a salt dissolves depends on the balance between the lattice enthalpy (energy needed to separate the ions of the solid) and the hydration enthalpies of the ions (energy released when water molecules surround them).

- **$\mathrm{K_2CO_3}$:** $\mathrm{K^+}$ is a large ion with a single charge, so the attraction between the ions in the lattice is relatively weak (low lattice enthalpy). The energy released on hydration of $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ is enough to overcome it, so the salt dissolves.
- **$\mathrm{CaCO_3}$:** $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ is smaller and carries a double charge (high charge density), so the electrostatic attraction between $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ is strong and the lattice enthalpy is high. The hydration enthalpies are not large enough to compensate for it, so calcium carbonate is insoluble.

**(iv)** In **excess** oxygen the heavier s-block metals form oxides richer in oxygen:

- **A. Potassium** forms the **superoxide**, potassium superoxide: $\mathrm{K(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{KO_2(s)}$ (orange-yellow solid).
- **B. Barium** forms the **peroxide**, barium peroxide: $\mathrm{Ba(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaO_2(s)}$.

(With a limited supply of oxygen the normal oxides form: $4\mathrm{K} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2O}$ and $2\mathrm{Ba} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{BaO}$. Large cations stabilise the large peroxide and superoxide anions.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give the symbols of the elements of the first transition series in order of increasing atomic number.

(ii) What accounts for the ability of transition metals to:

A: Show variable oxidation states

B: Form coloured compounds *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The first transition series (period 4, 3d block) is: **Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn** (atomic numbers 21 to 30; Sc and Zn are usually not counted as typical transition metals but are in the 3d series).

**(ii)**

**A. Variable oxidation states.** The **3d and 4s sub-shells are very close in energy**, so, after the 4s electrons, one or several 3d electrons can also be lost or used in bonding. The successive ionisation energies increase only gradually, so a range of oxidation states differing by one unit is accessible (for example Fe: +2 and +3; Mn: +2 to +7).

**B. Coloured compounds.** In the presence of ligands the five 3d orbitals split into two sets with a **small energy gap** between them. Transition metal ions have **partially filled d sub-shells**, so an electron can be promoted from the lower to the higher d level (a **d-d transition**) by absorbing light of the corresponding frequency in the visible region. The remaining (complementary) colours are transmitted, so the compound appears coloured.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Cobalt ($Z = 27$) forms a complex of formula $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]\mathrm{Br}$.

(i) Determine the oxidation state of cobalt in the complex

(ii) Using the electrons-in-boxes notation, write the electronic configuration of the cobalt ion in the complex

(iii) Draw the stereoisomers of $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]^+$ *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The complex ion is $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]^+$ (the bromide ion balances the $+1$ charge). $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is neutral and each chloride ligand is $-1$:

$$x + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = +3$$

The oxidation state of cobalt is **+3**.

**(ii)** Co: $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^7\,4s^2$. The ion $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$ has lost the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6$.

Electrons-in-boxes (4s empty; the six 3d electrons: one pair and four unpaired, by Hund's rule, for the free ion):

```
3d:  [ up/down ] [ up ] [ up ] [ up ] [ up ]      4s:  [    ]
```

(In the octahedral complex with the strong-field ligand $\mathrm{NH_3}$ the six d electrons pair up in the lower set of three orbitals, [ up/down ] [ up/down ] [ up/down ], leaving the upper two empty, so the complex is diamagnetic.)

**(iii) Stereoisomers.** $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]^+$ is octahedral (six ligands), and exists as two **geometric (cis-trans) isomers**:

```
trans: the two Cl are opposite (180 degrees)        cis: the two Cl are adjacent (90 degrees)

            Cl                                              Cl
            |                                               |
     H3N    |    NH3                                 H3N    |    Cl
        \   |   /                                       \   |   /
         \  |  /                                         \  |  /
          [ Co ]                                          [ Co ]
         /  |  \                                         /  |  \
        /   |   \                                       /   |   \
     H3N    |    NH3                                 H3N    |    NH3
            Cl                                              NH3
```

In the trans isomer the four $\mathrm{NH_3}$ lie in one plane with the two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ above and below it; in the cis isomer the two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ are next to each other (Cl-Co-Cl angle $90^\circ$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Contact process involves converting sulphur into its oxides, purifying and converting to sulphuric acid.

(i) Give equations for the formation of the oxides.

(ii) Why is the gas mixture purified?

(iii) State one industrial use of sulphuric acid. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Sulphur is burnt in air (or dry oxygen) to give sulphur dioxide, which is then oxidised to sulphur trioxide:

$$\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_2(g)}$$

$$2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -196\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\ (\text{per mole of the equation})$$

The second step is carried out over a **vanadium(V) oxide**, $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$, catalyst at about $450^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 to 2 atm. (The $\mathrm{SO_3}$ is then absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum, $\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}$, which is diluted with water to give $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.)

**(ii)** The mixture of gases must be purified (dust and impurities such as arsenic compounds removed) because the impurities would **poison the catalyst** ($\mathrm{V_2O_5}$ would be deactivated by being coated or by reacting), lowering the rate and the yield and making the process uneconomic.

**(iii)** One industrial use (any one): manufacture of **fertilisers** (ammonium sulphate and superphosphate); also in the manufacture of detergents, paints and pigments, fibres, plastics, in lead-acid car batteries, and in petroleum refining.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Complete the table below by giving the formula and name of a compound in which nitrogen exhibits the oxidation states +3 and +5. *[2 marks]*

| Oxidation state | Formula of compound | Name |
|---|---|---|
| +3 | | |
| +5 | | |
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Oxidation state | Formula of compound | Name |
|---|---|---|
| +3 | $\mathrm{HNO_2}$ | nitrous acid (nitric(III) acid) |
| +5 | $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ | nitric acid (nitric(V) acid) |

Check: in $\mathrm{HNO_2}$, $+1 + x + 2(-2) = 0$ gives $x = +3$; in $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, $+1 + x + 3(-2) = 0$ gives $x = +5$.

Other acceptable answers: for $+3$, $\mathrm{NaNO_2}$ (sodium nitrite, sodium nitrate(III)) or $\mathrm{N_2O_3}$ (dinitrogen trioxide); for $+5$, $\mathrm{NaNO_3}$ (sodium nitrate) or $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$ (dinitrogen pentoxide).
